item.text: {"case_id":"SPR00280","decision":"candidate","candidate_ranking":["C14","C02","C03"],"selected_candidate_label":"C14","confidence":0.97,"relationship_type":"both","rationale":"C14 plausibly supplied a concrete drafting template. Both memoranda begin by acknowledging the compelling appeal of helping severely disabled or blind people, then distinguish that appeal from the governing principle of an existing comprehensive benefit system. Each argues that the proposed categorical benefit would favor a less-needy subset at the expense of equitable treatment, undermine the system's foundational principle, and create an expansion with no logical stopping point. The recurrence of distinctive concepts such as self-reliance, a sound and comprehensive program, inequity to the most needy, and the absence of a stopping place is materially stronger than ordinary veto-message boilerplate. C02 and C03 share narrower special-exception-versus-uniform-system reasoning but lack C14's extensive parallel sequence and disability-benefit context.","shared_material":[{"child_excerpt":"our primary obligation to veterans disabled in the service... [is] assisting them to be as nearly as possible self-reliant and self-sustained members of society","parent_excerpt":"a genuine concern for the plight of blind persons and a desire to help them overcome their affliction and attain security to the maximum extent possible... useful and productive members of the community... self-reliance","explanation":"Both frame the ostensible benefit through the rehabilitative objective of independence and self-support."},{"child_excerpt":"A comprehensive program has already been adopted by the Government which is based squarely upon the policy of directly assisting the disabled veteran","parent_excerpt":"the unsound principle on which it is based would seriously hinder further progress in the development of a sound and comprehensive social security program","explanation":"Both defend an existing comprehensive assistance structure against a narrowly targeted addition that would compromise its organizing principle."},{"child_excerpt":"The practice of making gifts of special non-monetary benefits... to a particular group of disabled veterans, leads both to serious inequity and to abuse... a much larger number of veterans rated as high as 100 per cent disabled... will not receive automobiles","parent_excerpt":"This bill... would inevitably operate unfairly against those needy blind who are unable to work... [and] lead to reductions in the assistance payments of thousands of blind persons who are most in need","explanation":"Each develops the same distributive objection: a favored subgroup would receive additional benefits while more severely needy people remain excluded or disadvantaged."},{"child_excerpt":"it is not clear how or where we can stop this progressive expansion of the granting of automobiles short of providing one for every disabled veteran","parent_excerpt":"Once this principle has been breached, grave questions arise as to a logical stopping place... short of converting public assistance payments into flat, noncontributory pensions","explanation":"This is a distinctive parallel slippery-expansion formulation tied to abandoning the governing principle of the existing benefit system."}]}
